description:
Lone Rover is a focused project dedicated to tackling the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" challenge. 

Our goal is to design an intuitive, resilient health monitoring dashboard and early-warning system that tracks real-time vital signs, environmental stress factors, and operational readiness for astronauts during extended space missions.
summary:
We developed an offline, interactive biometric telemetry dashboard and predictive health simulator tailored for deep space missions. The platform features a live 1Hz telemetry stream, an interactive SVG body scanner, and a Mission Scenario Engine that models physiological degradation—such as osteopenia or fluid shifts—over 12 months across varying gravity fields (Microgravity/Mars) and EVA exertion.

To address the challenge, our tool empowers astronauts to conduct autonomous self-assessments. It integrates a gamified daily check-in routine, dynamic 30-day health trends, and live mapping to the 5 NASA HRP Spaceflight Hazards. Furthermore, it features an automated triage system that generates immediate SBAR flight-surgeon reports.

This solution is critical because, on long-duration missions to Mars, communication delays render real-time Earth support impossible. Astronauts require an intuitive, autonomous command center to instantly interpret complex health data, dispense medical countermeasures, and ensure crew survival without waiting for ground control.
details:
Overview & How It Works

Project Lone Rover is a comprehensive, offline-capable biometric telemetry dashboard and predictive health simulator designed for deep space habitats. It operates through a modern "progressive disclosure" UI. The primary view features an interactive SVG bio-scanner, allowing astronauts to click anatomical zones (Brain, Heart, Bones) to inspect streaming 1Hz telemetry. An advanced command hub expands to reveal a Mission Scenario Simulator that models physiological degradation—such as bone density loss—over a 12-month period across varying gravity fields (Microgravity vs. Mars) and EVA exertion.

Intended Impact & Benefits

During deep-space missions, Earth communication delays can take up to 20 minutes each way, rendering real-time medical support impossible. The impact of this project is to empower astronauts with autonomous medical independence. By providing immediate visual feedback and actionable countermeasures, astronauts can self-diagnose and stabilize critical conditions instantly without waiting for ground control.

Tools & Technologies Used

We built this project entirely from scratch as a two-person team using 100% Vanilla JavaScript, HTML5, and Custom CSS3. We intentionally avoided external libraries or frameworks to guarantee that the software remains lightweight, fast, and fully offline-capable in isolated space environments. Data persistence is handled locally via standard LocalStorage.

Creativity & Factors Considered

When designing the tool, our primary focus was mitigating "cognitive overload" during medical emergencies. The interface relies on strict status color-coding (Green/Yellow/Red) to convey urgency at a glance. We implemented an automated "Emergency Focus Mode" that triggers a dark-overlay screen with immediate stabilization steps if a biometric threshold is breached (e.g., HR > 120 BPM). Furthermore, we carefully considered the NASA Human Research Program's (HRP) 5 Hazards of Spaceflight, directly mapping them to a built-in Triage system that auto-generates SBAR flight-surgeon reports and gamifies the astronaut's daily health routine.
